passage: Urmila, why is your Hindi reader under the sofa? Too slow, you say? Dumb? Sit with your Nana. In Class 3, our teacher made us read aloud, row by row. When my turn came, I read like a bullock cart, every word a bump. One boy laughed. After that I told myself, 'Sumit, you are dumb,' and I stopped opening books at home. For a whole year. Then my uncle, the truck driver, started leaving me the sports page. 'Read me this, I forgot my glasses,' he'd say. One short report a day. Slowly the bumps got smaller. My reading was never dumb. It was just slow and needed practice. That one word cost me a year. Now get the book out and read me one page.

qa.q: What did Sumit's uncle leave for him to read?
qa.a: The uncle left Sumit the sports page.

qa.q: Why did Sumit stop opening books at home?
qa.a: After the boy laughed, Sumit felt ashamed and decided the whole problem was being dumb, so trying seemed pointless; the label hid the real issue of slow reading.

qa.q: What made the uncle's plan work?
qa.a: One short report a day, asked for as a favour, gave Sumit easy, regular practice without shame, so the reading skill could grow.

qa.q: What might Urmila feel hearing that Nana once called himself dumb?
qa.a: Urmila may feel less alone and a bit braver, seeing that slow reading can improve with practice, which makes one page tonight feel possible.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how, as a slow reader, he called himself dumb and stopped trying, until daily practice showed it was a skill.

passage: The power went out at seven, the night before the reading test, and the only light in the one-room flat was the emergency lamp. Naveen pushed the English reader away. 'I'm dumb. Everyone reads fast except me. What's the point?' Suraj bhaiya, who was supposed to be doing his own homework, pulled the lamp closer. 'You're not dumb. You're slow at long words. That's a different thing.' 'Same thing.' 'No. Dumb can't practise. Slow at long words can.' Suraj covered the page with his hand and showed one word at a time: 'ele-phant', 'bas-ket'. The lamp flickered. Naveen read 'basket' in one go and looked up, surprised. They did ten words before the battery died. In the dark Naveen said, 'Ten more tomorrow morning?'

qa.q: What light did they have during the power cut?
qa.a: The only light was the emergency lamp.

qa.q: Why does Naveen say 'What's the point?'
qa.a: Naveen feels ashamed of reading slowly and has turned it into 'I'm dumb', a fixed label, so trying feels useless.

qa.q: What did Suraj bhaiya do that changed things?
qa.a: He swapped the label for a specific skill, slow long words, and then practised it one word at a time, so Naveen could see progress within ten words.

qa.q: What is it like for Suraj to give up homework time in the dark?
qa.a: Suraj seems to care more about his sibling's confidence than his own homework, and may feel quietly glad when Naveen asks for ten more words.

grounding: Shows a child in a power cut who calls themselves dumb over slow reading, and an older brother who turns the label into a skill to practise.

passage: In the Tolichowki flat, Hafsa's reading homework lay open on the dining table while the pressure cooker whistled in the kitchen. She was stuck on the third line, the same line as yesterday. She shut the book hard. 'I'm stupid. Zainab reads a whole page before I finish one line.' Noor Apa looked up from her college notes. 'Which word stopped you?' 'All of them.' 'Show me one.' Hafsa pointed: 'through'. 'That's a tricky one. It doesn't sound how it looks. That's the word's fault, not yours.' Hafsa almost smiled. Noor wrote 'through', 'though' and 'thought' on a strip of paper. 'Five minutes on these three. That's all.' Hafsa glared at the strip, then picked up the pencil.

qa.q: Which word did Hafsa point to?
qa.a: Hafsa pointed to 'through'.

qa.q: Why does Hafsa call herself stupid?
qa.a: Hafsa is frustrated at being stuck on the same line and compares herself with Zainab, so one hard skill turns into a label about her whole self.

qa.q: What turning point did Noor Apa create?
qa.a: By asking which word stopped her and writing a strip of three similar words, Noor turned 'I'm stupid' into a small problem to practise, and Hafsa picked up the pencil.

qa.q: How might Noor Apa feel hearing her little sister say 'I'm stupid'?
qa.a: Noor Apa may feel sad hearing it and want to act quickly, which is why she puts down her own college notes to find the exact word.

grounding: Shows a child stuck on a reading line who calls herself stupid, and an older sister who narrows the label to one word to practise.

passage:
Rekha, eight, slammed the storybook shut on the bed.

"I'm dumb, Charu Mausi. I'm not reading anymore."

"Dumb? Who says?"

"Me. Pinky reads a whole page before I finish three lines."

"Hmm. Yesterday who read me the recipe for halwa?"

"...Me. But that was short."

"And who read the bus number from far away when I couldn't?"

"That's numbers."

"So you can read short things and numbers. Is that dumb?"

Rekha folded her arms. "It's long pages. Long pages hate me."

"Ah. So it's not 'dumb'. It's 'long pages are slow for me'. That's a different problem. Slow things get faster with practice."

"No, they don't."

"Let's check. One page tonight. I'll time you. Then same page on Friday."

Rekha didn't answer. But she pulled the book back from the pillow and opened it on her knees.

qa.q: Who read the recipe for halwa to Charu Mausi yesterday?
qa.a: Rekha did.

qa.q: Why does calling herself "dumb" feel easier to Rekha than keeping going?
qa.a: Comparing herself with Pinky makes her feel ashamed, and "dumb" explains everything at once. If she's dumb, there's no point trying, so stopping feels like relief.

qa.q: What turning point did Charu Mausi create with her questions?
qa.a: By pointing out Rekha can read recipes and bus numbers, Mausi changed "dumb" into a specific skill, reading long pages, that can be practised. Timing one page tonight and again on Friday makes improvement something Rekha can see.

qa.q: How might Charu Mausi feel hearing an eight-year-old call herself dumb?
qa.a: Charu Mausi might feel a pang of worry and want to protect Rekha from that word sticking. Her patient questions suggest she wants Rekha to see herself more fairly.

grounding: A girl who reads long pages slowly calls herself dumb and stops trying, while her aunt helps her see a specific skill that can be practised.

passage:
I'm Aadhya and I'm eleven now. When I was eight, I thought I was lazy and dumb, because reading took me forever. The others finished the chapter and I was still on the first page, sounding words in my head.

So I stopped. If I was dumb, why try? I hid the reader in my school bag and said I'd forgotten it.

My friend Ira didn't believe it. One day she brought comics to my house. "Read me the bubbles," she said. "Only the bubbles." The bubbles were short, so I could. We read the whole comic. It took ages, but we laughed a lot.

We did that every Saturday. Slowly, my eyes got faster.

Now I know I wasn't dumb or lazy. I was just slow at reading, and slow can be practised. I still read slower than Ira. But I read.

qa.q: What did Ira ask Aadhya to read in the comics?
qa.a: "Read me the bubbles. Only the bubbles."

qa.q: Why did Aadhya stop trying to read at eight?
qa.a: Aadhya believed the words dumb and lazy, so trying felt pointless. The label made reading seem like something impossible, not something that could be practised.

qa.q: Which choice of Ira's worked, and why?
qa.a: Starting with short speech bubbles in a fun comic let Aadhya succeed and enjoy reading. Practising every Saturday built the actual skill that the label had hidden.

qa.q: What might Ira have noticed that made her not believe the label?
qa.a: Ira probably saw that Aadhya could read, just slowly, and was hiding the reader rather than being unable. Ira seemed to see a friend who needed practice, not a dumb person.

grounding: A child who read slowly took on the label dumb and stopped trying, until a friend helped with practising the specific skill the label had hidden.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today in reading time Miss made us read out loud. When it was my turn I got stuck on 'enormous' and 'caterpillar'. Everyone waited. Neelam read her page so fast, like water. I'm dumb. That's just what I am. Neelam is the clever one and I'm the dumb one.
At home Amma gave me the new storybook with the elephant on the cover. I didn't even open it. What's the point? Dumb people can't read big books. I put it under my bed.
Amma asked why. I said I'm too dumb. She looked sad and said we'll read one page together tomorrow. I said maybe.
Vidya

qa.q: Which words did Vidya get stuck on?
qa.a: Vidya got stuck on 'enormous' and 'caterpillar'.

qa.q: Why did Vidya put the new storybook under the bed?
qa.a: Vidya felt embarrassed and discouraged after getting stuck in class, and deciding 'I'm dumb' made trying seem pointless.

qa.q: How could Amma help Vidya turn 'dumb' into a skill to practise?
qa.a: Amma could read one page together and show that long words like 'caterpillar' can be practised, so the problem is a skill, not who Vidya is.

qa.q: How might Neelam see Vidya's reading?
qa.a: Neelam may not have noticed much, since everyone gets stuck sometimes, and would probably be surprised to hear Vidya use the word 'dumb'.

grounding: A child who reads slowly calls themselves dumb and stops trying, letting a label replace a skill that can be practised.

passage: Every evening, the children of Bhadrajun sat on the temple steps to read their Hindi lessons aloud while the goats were brought home. Hansa always finished last. Her finger moved slowly under each word, and when her younger cousin Darshan read the same page in half the time, she shut her book with a slap. 'I'm a buddhu. Buddhus shouldn't read,' she said, and went to help with the goats instead. The next evening she didn't bring her book at all. Darshan came and sat by her anyway. 'You read the long word yesterday. Pradhanmantri. I can't even say it,' he said. Hansa shrugged. 'That was luck.' But she watched his finger on the page for a long time, her lips moving.

qa.q: Where did the children of Bhadrajun read their lessons?
qa.a: They read their Hindi lessons aloud on the temple steps.

qa.q: Why did Hansa call herself a buddhu and go to the goats?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and frustrated at always finishing last, and the label made stopping feel easier than facing slow reading again.

qa.q: What could an adult do to help Hansa see reading as a skill?
qa.a: They could have her practise a few words each day and point out progress, like reading 'Pradhanmantri', so the label gives way to a skill that grows.

qa.q: How does Darshan see Hansa's reading?
qa.a: Darshan admires that she read a long word he couldn't say, and sits with her to show she isn't a buddhu.

grounding: A village child who reads slowly calls herself a fool and stops bringing her book, letting a label replace a skill she could practise.

passage: On library day at the primary school in Melbourne, everyone in Jin's class had to choose a chapter book. Oskar grabbed one about dragons with three hundred pages. Jin picked it up after him, read the first line twice, and put it back. 'I'm too stupid for chapter books,' he told the librarian, and chose a picture book about trucks he'd read before. Back at his desk, during quiet reading, he turned the pages without really looking. When Ms Tran asked him to try the first page of the dragon book with her, he shook his head. 'I'm just slow. I'm always going to be slow.' Ms Tran didn't argue. She put a bookmark in the dragon book at page two and left it on his desk.

qa.q: What book did Jin choose instead of a chapter book?
qa.a: He chose a picture book about trucks he'd read before.

qa.q: Why did Jin choose the truck book he had already read?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and embarrassed after reading the first line twice, and calling himself stupid made avoiding the hard book feel safe.

qa.q: What was clever about Ms Tran's bookmark?
qa.a: It made the task tiny and specific, just one page, which treats reading as a skill to practise rather than a verdict on Jin.

qa.q: What would change if Jin saw 'slow' as a skill to practise?
qa.a: He might try a page a day of the dragon book, and in time reading would get easier instead of becoming a reason to stop.

grounding: A child who reads slowly calls himself stupid and avoids chapter books, letting a label replace a skill that can be practised.

passage:
In the school library's reading hour, Gopika closed her book after one page. "I'm dumb," she told Eshaan, the Class 7 reading buddy. "Everyone else is on chapter three. I'm dumb at reading. So I'm not doing it."

Eshaan looked at the page. "Which word stopped you?"
"All of them."
"Show me one."
She pointed. "Th-rough."
"Ah, 'through'. That's a sneaky word. The 'gh' is silent. That's not dumb, that's one tricky spelling." He wrote it on a sticky note. "Want to collect sneaky words? Every one you find is a point."

Gopika opened the book again, suspicious. By the end of the hour she had four sticky notes and had finished page three.

qa.q: Which word did Gopika point to?
qa.a: Gopika pointed to "through".

qa.q: Why did Gopika stop trying after one page?
qa.a: Gopika felt embarrassed and discouraged about reading slowly, and the label "dumb" made trying seem pointless.

qa.q: How did Eshaan turn the label into a skill?
qa.a: He asked for one hard word, explained the silent "gh", and made tricky words into a game she could practise.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel as the sticky notes pile up?
qa.a: Eshaan probably feels pleased and proud to see Gopika reading again.

grounding: Shows a girl who reads slowly calling herself dumb and giving up, until a reading buddy turns the label into a skill.

passage:
Monday: when Ms Sarita asked Darshan to read the paragraph aloud, he said, "I can't, I'm stupid at reading." The class went quiet. He read nothing that day.

Wednesday: Ms Sarita kept him back. "You said stupid. What exactly is hard?" Darshan thought. "Long words. And I lose my place." "That's two things," she said. "Not stupid. Two things. We can practise two things." She gave him a ruler to keep his place and a list of five long words to break into parts: "hap-pen-ing".

Friday: Darshan read three lines aloud, the ruler under each line. He stumbled on "adventure", stopped, broke it up, "ad-ven-ture", and went on. When he sat down, he didn't say stupid. He said, "I lost my place once."

qa.q: What did Ms Sarita give Darshan to keep his place?
qa.a: Ms Sarita gave Darshan a ruler.

qa.q: Why did Darshan say "I'm stupid at reading"?
qa.a: Darshan felt embarrassed and discouraged, and a single label felt easier than naming what was hard.

qa.q: What did Ms Sarita do that replaced the label?
qa.a: She asked exactly what was hard, named two skills, long words and losing his place, and gave him a ruler and word-breaking practice.

qa.q: How might the class see Darshan on Friday?
qa.a: They see him read three lines and keep going after a stumble, a change from Monday's silence.

grounding: Over a week a boy who calls himself stupid at reading learns to name two specific skills he can practise.

passage:
Jasleen, you called yourself lazy again today. Come, your Nikita Nani will tell you something. When I was nine, in Dehradun, I couldn't learn my tables. Everyone else sang them like songs. I got stuck after seven sixes. So I decided: I'm lazy. Lazy girls don't learn tables. And I stopped trying. Why try, if you're lazy?

My grandfather heard me say it. He didn't argue. He asked, "Which table, exactly?" I said the sevens and eights. He said, "That's not lazy. That's two tables." Every evening he wrote one line on a matchbox, and we practised it walking to the temple.

By Diwali I knew them. I still say "seven sixes are forty-two" when I climb stairs. So, Jasleen, which part exactly is hard?

qa.q: Which tables did young Nikita find hard?
qa.a: The sevens and eights.

qa.q: Why did young Nikita stop trying?
qa.a: Young Nikita felt discouraged and ashamed, and calling herself lazy made trying seem pointless.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed things?
qa.a: Her grandfather asked, "Which table, exactly?", turned the label into two tables, and practised one line with her each evening.

qa.q: How might Nikita's grandfather have felt hearing "I'm lazy"?
qa.a: He was probably saddened but calm, choosing a question and patient practice over an argument.

grounding: A grandmother recalls calling herself lazy as a girl who struggled with times tables, until the label became two tables to practise.

passage: The Sankranti holidays came with cold nights and long power cuts. Irawati sat by the lantern with her reading book while her brother Akash did sums. The words swam in the yellow light. She read "though" as "through" and stopped. "I'm so stupid. I can't read anything." She shut the book. Akash looked up. "You read that whole page yesterday." "Because it was easy. I'm dumb at reading." Their grandmother, knitting in the corner, said, "Stupid is a big word for a small thing. Which word stopped you?" Irawati pointed. "This one." "Then that's the one to practise. Not your whole head." Ajji wrote "though" and "through" on a slate, side by side. Irawati read them three times. Then she opened the book again, slowly, by the flickering lantern.

qa.q: Which word did Irawati read wrongly?
qa.a: She read "though" as "through".

qa.q: Why did Irawati shut the book and call herself stupid?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and ashamed at the mistake, and one label seemed to sum up everything about her reading.

qa.q: What did Ajji do that helped Irawati start again?
qa.a: Ajji turned "stupid" into one specific word to practise, writing both words on a slate so Irawati could master them.

qa.q: How might Akash see his sister calling herself dumb?
qa.a: Akash seemed surprised, since he had seen her read a whole page the day before.

grounding: During a winter festival a girl who reads slowly by lantern calls herself stupid and stops, until a grandmother points to one specific word to practise.

passage: A week before Diwali, Class 4 in the Ghatkopar school had a reading circle. Trisha's turn came. She read slowly, finger under each word. Someone sighed. By the third line, her face was hot. She put the book down. "I'm dumb. I can't read. Skip me." At home that evening, she refused to help her cousin Swati read out the names on the Diwali gift tags. "I'm stupid at reading. Everyone knows." Swati didn't argue. She held up a tag. "Just this one word. Mausi." Trisha read it. "And this one?" "Chacha." "See? You're not stupid. You're slow at long words. That's a thing you can practise." Trisha looked at the pile of tags. "Only the short ones," she said, and picked up a pen.

qa.q: What did Swati ask Trisha to read?
qa.a: Swati asked her to read the names on the Diwali gift tags.

qa.q: Why did Trisha refuse to read and call herself dumb?
qa.a: Trisha felt embarrassed after someone sighed in class, and calling herself stupid felt easier than facing the slow reading.

qa.q: How did Swati help Trisha see the problem differently?
qa.a: Swati showed her she could read short words and named the real issue as slowness with long words, a skill to practise.

qa.q: What would change if Swati had simply said, "You're not dumb"?
qa.a: Trisha might not have believed it; reading the tags herself gave her proof.

grounding: Near Diwali a girl who reads slowly calls herself dumb and stops trying, until a cousin turns the label back into a skill to practise.

passage:
"Tushar, your turn to read."
"No, didi. I'm stupid at reading."
"Who said that?"
"Me. I'm the slowest in summer reading club."
Nirmala didi put the book down on the mat. "Slow and stupid aren't the same."
"They are for me."
"Okay. What happens when you read?"
"The long words get stuck."
"All of them?"
"...The ones with 'tion'."
"Like station?"
"Station. Yes."
"So you can read station."
"Only because you said it first."
"Then let's make a list of 'tion' words. You read them. I won't say them first."
"And if I get them wrong?"
"Then we'll know exactly what to practise. Not that you're stupid."
Tushar pulled the paper toward him. "Na... tion. Nation." He looked up. "That wasn't that bad."

qa.q: Which long words get stuck for Tushar?
qa.a: The ones with 'tion'.

qa.q: Why did Tushar say he was stupid at reading?
qa.a: Tushar felt ashamed of being the slowest in reading club, so one label seemed to explain everything.

qa.q: How did Nirmala didi help Tushar move from a label to a skill?
qa.a: She asked exactly which words got stuck, then made a list of 'tion' words for Tushar to practise without her saying them first.

qa.q: What might Nirmala didi feel when Tushar read "Nation"?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased and encouraged that he tried and saw the problem was smaller than he thought.

grounding: In summer reading club a boy calls himself stupid at reading, and a helper turns the label into a specific skill to practise.

passage:
In the summer holidays, Sangeeta Didi from upstairs started a reading club on the terrace. Everyone had to read one page aloud. When it was my turn, the words came out slow and wobbly, and Rohit finished his page before I finished my first line. So I closed the book and said, "I'm dumb. I can't read."
I didn't go back the next day. Or the next. Didi came down to our flat and asked why. I said, "Because I'm stupid at reading."
She said, "You're not stupid, Yogesh. You're slow at long words. That's a thing we can practise."
I didn't believe her. But I liked that she came down.

qa.q: Who started the reading club?
qa.a: Sangeeta Didi from upstairs.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh stop going to the reading club?
qa.a: Yogesh felt embarrassed and ashamed after reading slowly next to Rohit, and deciding "I'm dumb" made trying again feel pointless.

qa.q: What could help Yogesh keep trying?
qa.a: Practising long words a few at a time with Didi, perhaps reading with her alone first, so the specific skill grows instead of the label.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta see Yogesh's reading?
qa.a: She sees a child who is slow at long words, not stupid, and cares enough to come down and say so.

grounding: A child who reads slowly calls themselves dumb and stops going, and an older neighbour names the specific skill to practise.
